title: what carries on?
hook: if there's no soul packed up and moved, what goes on? one flame lighting the next

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vesak, and a person who woke up. Six words so far: karma, the three jewels, sati, the four noble truths, dana, Vesak. Today, the seventh.
screen: `KARMA · THE THREE JEWELS · SATI · THE FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS · DANA · VESAK`

segments.voice: When a grandparent dies, many Buddhist families do more than hold a funeral. Monks chant. Food is offered, and the good of it is dedicated to the one who died. In many East Asian and Tibetan communities, the prayers go on for forty-nine days, a time, those traditions say, between one life and the next. Behind it is the question day one left hanging: when a life ends, what happens to everything it set growing? And there's a twist. In the Buddha's teaching, no fixed soul packs up and moves.
screen: `A GRANDPARENT DIES.` → `FORTY-NINE DAYS OF PRAYERS.` → `WHAT GOES ON?`

segments.voice: Many Buddhist traditions teach rebirth: a life, when it ends, is followed by another, shaped by karma, round and round, until someone wakes up. Teachers often prefer the word rebirth to reincarnation, because nothing solid moves across. An old book of questions gives the best-known picture. A king asks a monk: is the one who's reborn the same person, or someone else? Neither, says the monk. Light one lamp from another. Did the flame move over? No. Is the new flame unrelated? No again: it was lit from the first. So what passes on is momentum, not a soul. Traditions describe the details very differently: how, where, how soon. Some teachers also point to a version anyone can watch: each moment lit from the last. And for anyone unsure about all of it, there's an old answer too. The Buddha once spoke to villagers who didn't know which teachers to believe. A kind, clear life is good either way, he told them: if there's another life, it goes well; if there isn't, this one already does.
screen: `REBIRTH, NOT A SOUL MOVING HOUSE` · `SAME PERSON? NEITHER, NOR ANOTHER` · `ONE LAMP LIGHTS ANOTHER` · `GOOD EITHER WAY` · then, large: `ONE FLAME LIGHTS THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, notice this breath arriving. On the second, notice that it isn't the one before, and that it came from the one before. On the third, let it go, and let the next one light itself.
Rebirth. Not a soul moving house: one flame lighting the next, carried by karma. Seventh word, and a week's worth.
Your line: one flame lights the next. That's week one: seven words, from a meme to a lamp. Tomorrow, the word behind the first truth.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists understand death as followed by rebirth shaped by karma, and mark a death with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites (in many communities over the following seven weeks); traditions describe the process differently, and some teachers also apply it to moment-to-moment experience.

fork.setup: a king asks a monk: is the one who's reborn the same person, or someone else? what does the monk answer, in the old book of questions?
options: neither: like a lamp lit from a lamp.
fork.reveal: neither the same nor another. the new flame didn't move over, but it was lit from the first.

original.note: Pali: rebirth, literally 'becoming again'. puna, again; bhava, becoming.

trapdoor: what you thought: reincarnation, a soul moving into a new body.
what it means: a new life lit from the old one by karma, with no fixed self carried across.

what a scholar hears: punabbhava, renewed becoming. the Milindapañha answers 'neither the same nor another' (na ca so na ca añño) and uses the lamp lit from a lamp; schools differ on the intermediate state (antarābhava) and the mechanism.

story.title: the king and the chariot
story.text: A king who has beaten every debater in his kingdom sits down across from a monk named Nagasena and asks his name. Nagasena, the monk says, but that's only a label: no fixed person is found behind it. The king pounces: then who am I talking to? The monk asks how the king came. By chariot. Is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The seat? No, no, no, says the king, it's the name for all the parts together. Exactly, says Nagasena.
story.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda) II.1.1

wrong.myth: Buddhist rebirth is a soul moving into a new body.
wrong.truth: many teachers say nothing fixed moves across. a new life is lit from the old, like a flame from a flame: neither the same nor someone else.

build.prompt: build the Pali word: again + becoming.

notes: New lesson, written 2026-10-06 for the rebuilt week one (audience research's day 7: 'what continues? rebirth, gently, without picking one school's metaphysics'). It closes the loop with day 1's karma.

The king's question and the lamp combine two passages of the Milindapanha: 'neither the same nor another' (II.2.1, where the image is a lamp burning through the night) and rebirth without transmigration (III.5.5, a lamp lit from another lamp). Confirm the combination and section numbers (Rhys Davids, SBE 35).
'Teachers often prefer the word rebirth to reincarnation, because nothing solid moves across': a common teaching distinction; confirm.

The moment-to-moment reading is credited to 'some teachers', not given as the teaching. Schools differ on the intermediate state and the mechanism; the script names only the shared shape. Confirm this is fair to Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana readers.

Added 2026-10-06 from the Reddit research (rebirth is the deal-breaker doubt for Western-raised seekers; heritage families keep the rites for the dead): the hook now opens on a family's rites after a grandparent dies, and the teach ends with the Kalama Sutta's assurances (AN 3.65): if there is another world, a person free of hostility arises well; if not, they live at ease here and now. Paraphrased as 'a kind, clear life is good either way'; the text is not named. Confirm the paraphrase; some Keepers may want to add that rebirth is part of right view in the discourses.

The 49-day period between death and rebirth is taught in Tibetan (bardo) and much of East Asian Buddhism; Theravada generally does not teach an intermediate state, though Theravada families hold merit-making rites (e.g., on the seventh day). The hook says 'in many East Asian and Tibetan communities' and 'those traditions say'. Confirm.
Dedicating the good of an offering to the dead (merit transfer, pattidana) is described generally. Confirm.
Nirvana is no longer mentioned here; it is opened on day 10.
howItsDone mentions memorial rites 'over the following seven weeks' (the 49-day observance) as 'in many communities'. Confirm.
